strengths: AVIS addresses a meaningful gap between audio-visual semantic segmentation and video instance segmentation: distinguishing sounding instances of the same category while maintaining their identities across changes in sound activity. This is a useful contribution to multimodal video understanding.

AVISeg is a substantial resource: 926 videos averaging 61.4 seconds, 56,871 annotated frames, and 94,074 instance masks across 26 categories. Its inclusion of silent, single-source, and multi-source frames supports research beyond conventional short-clip segmentation. The dataset contribution and supported baseline results make the overall balance favor weak acceptance.

The main comparison provides evidence on established metrics independently of the proposed FSLA metric. With the reported common ResNet-50 initialization and training budget, AVISM reaches 61.73 HOTA and 40.57 mAP, versus 57.48/36.25 for VITA and 57.39/37.84 for COMBO (Table 2). These are meaningful improvements in joint segmentation and tracking.

The architecture is technically plausible, and the ablations support its audio-fusion components. Adding video-level fusion to frame-level fusion improves HOTA from 59.59 to 61.73 and mAP from 39.06 to 40.57 (Table 4). Window-size and similarity-loss studies provide additional evidence. The supplement supplies training settings, baseline prompts, qualitative comparisons, and informative failure cases.
weaknesses: The FSLA specification has consequential reproducibility problems. Algorithm 1 credits silent frames without checking for false-positive predictions, initializes counters outside the IoU-threshold loop, and does not explicitly enforce the required object-count and all-instance correctness conditions. Its aggregation also does not implement the stated class averaging. Thus, the pseudocode cannot reproduce the intended metric as written. This leaves the reported FSLA results insufficiently specified, although it does not establish that the actual implementation or separate HOTA/mAP results are incorrect.

Dataset quality assurance is underdocumented for the task's hardest labels. Section 4 describes SAM-assisted masks and repeated manual review, but gives no quantitative annotation audit or agreement measurements, nor detailed rules for resolving ambiguous simultaneous sound sources and sound transitions within one-second intervals. Source grouping or duplicate checks across the random splits are also unspecified. These omissions limit assessment of the benchmark's reliability without demonstrating that its annotations or splits are defective.

The conclusions about multimodal large models exceed what the adaptation protocols establish. Supplement E merges same-category masks into one identity for Sam4AVS and BuboGPT, treats each category as one instance for AL-Ref-SAM 2, and uses only the top audio class for Sam4AVS. These choices directly restrict performance on the defining same-category, multi-instance cases. Table 3 demonstrates limitations of these particular pipelines, rather than isolating general failures of multimodal reasoning.

The central same-category instance challenge receives insufficient targeted quantitative analysis. FSLAm groups all multi-source frames together, whereas Figure 10 explicitly shows failures with multiple people, tubas, and dogs. Results stratified by same-category multiplicity and sound-activity changes would be more diagnostic than the current aggregate scores. The music-heavy distribution and 1-FPS evaluation also constrain conclusions about broader scenes and precise temporal localization.

The model's originality is primarily its adaptation to the new task: object-token association, shifted windows, and much of the segmentation machinery follow Mask2Former/VITA/Swin. Moreover, Table 5 measures maximum frame capacity, but provides no comparative runtime or memory measurements and no accuracy analysis across video durations. The evidence therefore supports a useful baseline more strongly than the broader claims of superior long-range modeling and computational practicality.
